name: Dirty Green
lede: Dirty Green is a muted olive-leaning green, a plain descriptive name more than a pigment or dye.

sections.title: A plain description
sections.body:
Our earliest record of Dirty Green as a color name is the xkcd list of 2010 [3]. The words are much older. A passage quoted by Ball tells how verditer makers sometimes got a fair blue and sometimes only a dirtier green from the same materials, with no rule they could name [1]. Schoenberg's score for *Die glückliche Hand* calls for lights changing from a dull red to yellow, then through dirty green, violet, blue-grey and blood red [2]. And the pigment literature uses the phrase for a precipitate: when arsenic was added to dissolved verdigris in the early nineteenth century, a dirty green solid formed first, before being redissolved to give a bright green [4].

In Ball's passage the phrase marks a green that went wrong [1]. In Gage it is one stage in a light-score [2]. In the pigment text it is a step in a process [4]. The modern swatch borrows an everyday phrase [3].

Its nearest neighbors among our names, by CIELAB distance, are [[moss-olive|Moss olive]], [[khaki-green|Khaki Green]] and [[sap-green|Sap Green]] [5]. On a white page it reaches a contrast ratio of 4.58:1 [5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Dirty Green appears in 74 of 23,781 paintings, 0.31%, as photographed [6]. It most often plays an accent, in 66% of the 47 paintings where the within-painting reading finds it [6]. It peaks in the 1900s at 2.6 times the expected rate (10 paintings), and it is most over-represented in French paintings, at 2.2 times (19 of 3,443) [6]. Sargent painted it most often (4 of 287 works here), though no painter stands out against the baseline [6].
